notes.heading: Distinguish concession, correction and sequence
paragraphs: Transitions describe the logical relationship between propositions. Concession retains a difficulty while stating an unexpected outcome. Correction replaces or narrows an earlier idea, while a time transition only orders events. Choosing a transition cannot supply evidence that the surrounding sentences lack. Read the two claims without the transition, state their relationship in plain language, then select a word that expresses that relationship. Finally check punctuation: a conjunctive adverb does not by itself join two independent clauses with a comma.

questions.prompt: Original fictional text: 'The trail was steep. ___, the group reached the shelter before sunset.' Choose Nevertheless or Consequently and explain the implied expectation.
questions.answer: Nevertheless fits: the steep trail might have delayed the group, yet they arrived before sunset.
solution: Identify the obstacle and the outcome that runs against its expected effect.
Consequently would suggest the steepness caused timely arrival, which the text does not support.

questions.prompt: Original fictional text: 'The box contains no metal tools. ___, it holds only wooden models.' Choose Instead or Meanwhile and justify the relationship.
questions.answer: Instead fits because the second statement supplies the alternative contents; Meanwhile would introduce a time relationship.
solution: Compare what the box does not contain with what it actually contains.
Select the replacement relationship, not simultaneity.

questions.prompt: Original fictional text: 'The library extended its hours in March. By April, recorded visits had risen.' Add one transition that preserves timing without asserting cause, and state what a causal claim would additionally need.
questions.answer: Subsequently is one possible transition. A causal claim needs evidence addressing alternatives such as seasonal demand, publicity or changes in counting.
solution: Use a temporal link rather than therefore.
State a comparison or evidence that would separate the extended-hours effect from other changes.
markingPoints: Avoid treating sequence as proof of cause.
Name an alternative and useful additional evidence.
